cim: Billionaire David Tepper Dumped Appaloosa's Stake in AMD and Broadcom and Piled Into an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Stock Trading at 44x Forward Adjusted EPS
cim_eredeti: Billionaire David Tepper Dumped Appaloosa's Stake in AMD and Broadcom and Piled Into an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Stock Trading at 44x Forward Adjusted EPS
szoveg_eredeti:
David Tepper has been one of the most successful hedge fund managers over the past three-plus decades.

After leaving Goldman Sachs in 1993, he founded Appaloosa Management, which, according to Bloomberg News, generated compound annual returns of 25% until 2019. That year, Tepper announced plans to convert Appaloosa into a family office, and the fund still files 13F quarterly reports. Given Tepper's track record, investors pay close attention to these filings.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

As I've said in the past, blindly following investments from a 13F is a poor substitute for your own research, given 13F filings show only positions a fund held on the last day of the quarter, arrive weeks after that quarter ended, and don't explain why the fund bought that position. However, 13Fs are a good source for new investment ideas, or a way to validate an existing investment thesis.

In the third quarter, Appaloosa exited its positions in AMD and Broadcom while piling into an artificial intelligence stock trading at roughly 44 times forward adjusted earnings per share.

David Tepper. Image source: Getty Images.

The filing shows Appaloosa exited all 197,500 AMD shares and all 150,000 Broadcom shares.

While we can only speculate, the third quarter was rough for AI chip stocks. In July, the MSCI World Semiconductor Index fell about 13%, its worst month since 2022, as investors questioned potential returns from AI capital investment. Rising interest rates may have added to the pressure, as higher yields often hit highly valued growth stocks hardest.

Company-specific news may have played a role, too. AMD reported strong second-quarter results on Aug. 4, with revenue up 50% and data center sales more than doubling. Management also provided forward guidance above Wall Street consensus estimates. Yet the stock fell sharply immediately after the report due to lofty market expectations and a lack of margin expansion.

Broadcom's Sept. 2 earnings report showed a similar pattern. AI semiconductor revenue rocketed 221% higher to $16.7 billion, but fourth-quarter revenue guidance of $34.8 billion landed slightly below consensus, and the stock took a hit as well.

This shows how, at the time, valuations left little room for error. Tepper, like many others, may simply have been taking profits, on the belief that the AI trade and several stocks deeply intertwined with it needed to catch their breath.

While Tepper was selling some AI stocks, he was piling into others. Appaloosa opened a small position in Space Exploration Technologies (NASDAQ:SPCX) in the second quarter.

In the third quarter, the fund increased its stake by 1,626%, ending the quarter with over 3.8 million shares. At the end of the third quarter, the stake was worth $557 million, or about 7.4% of its reported portfolio.

SpaceX went public in June at $135 per share in the largest IPO at the time, and while shares have been volatile, they trade at roughly the same level as of this writing.

SpaceX has become a battleground stock. The company has an impressive group of businesses, including its launch business, which leverages mostly reusable rockets to conduct space expeditions more quickly and cost-effectively than before.

SpaceX also offers a low earth orbit satellite internet service called Starlink that can provide high-speed internet to people with limited access to traditional internet infrastructure. Starlink had over 13.6 million paying subscribers at the end of the third quarter.

Finally, there is SpaceX's sprawling AI division, which includes multiple data centers with significant compute capacity, the social platform X, and a planned future Terafab facility, among other AI initiatives.

The question is how much you believe SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk's ambitious agenda. On the company's most recent earnings call, Musk said SpaceX had 1.7 gigawatts (GW) of compute provided by its data centers at the end of the third quarter and expects to reach 2.5 GW to 3 GW by year-end.

Then, Musk said he's highly confident the company can bring another 10 GW of compute online by the end of 2027, and potentially as much as 20 GW. Even achieving the 10 GW would be an astounding accomplishment.

Wall Street analysts think the company will grow revenue quickly, and are now projecting about $181 billion of revenue in 2027, up from a projected $49 billion this year. They also project $4.21 in adjusted EPS for 2027, implying SpaceX trades at slightly over 44x adjusted EPS.

The market may not fully buy into it, and achieving this will require significant capital expenditures and likely result in significantly negative free cash flow.

Still, if SpaceX achieves even the 10 GW of additional compute, I suspect the stock will perform well. Tepper seems to believe Musk, or at the very least that the stock near IPO levels can swing higher in the near term.
